subject: Art & Design
title: Reflections: Using Mirrors, Water, and Glass
description: One-minute skill: Reflections: Using Mirrors, Water, and Glass.

hook.text: A city reflected in a rain puddle creates two worlds in one frame. The reflection doubles the story.

buildup.text: Reflections add symmetry, depth, and surreal quality: water, glass windows, mirrors, and polished surfaces.

discovery.text: Shooting reflections often works best when flipped — the reflection becomes the main subject.

twist.text: Polarizing filters can remove reflections. But sometimes the reflection is the photo — don't filter it out.

climax.text: After rain, every city becomes a mirror. Puddle photography is an entire sub-genre of street photography.

punchline.text: Reflections don't copy reality. They reinterpret it.

quiz.question: When can a polarizing filter hurt your photograph?
options: When the reflection itself is the creative subject you want to capture
Only when shooting in direct sunlight

details.summary: Reflections in water, glass, mirrors, and polished surfaces create natural doubles that add symmetry, depth, and visual intrigue to photographs. Perfect reflections produce mirror-image compositions; imperfect reflections (rippled water, clouded glass) add abstract, dreamlike qualities.
details.whyItMatters: Reflections multiply visual content without adding complexity. They create compositions impossible through other techniques — reversed worlds, phantom architecture, and doubled landscapes that engage viewers with their visual trickery.
takeaways: Reflections create natural symmetry and visual doubles
Perfect reflections mirror scenes; imperfect ones add abstraction
Water, glass, and polished surfaces offer reflection opportunities

faq.question: How do you get perfect water reflections?
faq.answer: Shoot at calm water during windless conditions — early morning is best. Get low to the water's edge to maximize the reflection area in the frame. Use a polarizing filter to control reflection intensity. Perfectly still water near the edges produces mirror-like reflections most reliably.

faq.question: Should the real scene or its reflection be the focus?
faq.answer: Either can work. Some photographers split the frame 50/50 for pure symmetry. Others emphasize the reflection as the main subject, with the real scene as context. Upside-down reflection images — rotated 180 degrees — create surreal, disorienting compositions that challenge perception.
